issues.item: Threat: Risky Behavior: Taking too many risks or doing things that could cause you harm
issues.explanation: Risky behavior is hard to reconcile with the rest of the threat profile, which is dominated by fear-based hypervigilance and exaggerated startle. In this profile it introduces a more externalizing response pattern that is not supported elsewhere in memory, appraisals, triggers, or strategies.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: Betrayal by a trusted person does not fit well with the stated trauma type of civilian in a war zone unless there is evidence of an interpersonal betrayal trauma, which is otherwise absent from the profile. The rest of the items center on war exposure, victims, grief, loss of control, and danger rather than trusted-person betrayal.

issues.item: Triggers: Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
issues.explanation: Reminders of victims fit war-zone exposure, but paired with perpetrator-focused avoidance and betrayal appraisals they imply a specific interpersonal-harm narrative that is not otherwise coherently represented. The profile oscillates between mass-trauma civilian exposure and a perpetrator-betrayal formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: Avoiding cues related to the person who harmed me implies a discrete perpetrator-centered trauma. That is difficult to integrate with the rest of the profile, which more strongly reflects civilian war-zone exposure, victims, grief, and generalized threat rather than a single identifiable assailant.

vignette: Raj was a painter who had been living in a war-torn region when the conflict reached his home. He vividly remembered the day an explosion occurred near his house. The blast shattered windows and tore through walls, leaving him with fragmented memories of the chaos and destruction that followed. Since then, Raj has found himself constantly on edge. The smell of smoke or burning debris can instantly transport Raj back to those terrifying moments. When he encounters these scents in his daily life—like when a neighbor is barbecuing—he feels his body tense up as if he's right back there. This olfactory trigger not only brings him back to the event but also ignites his hypervigilance, making him feel superalert and ready to react to any danger that might come next. Raj’s experiences of loss of control during the explosion are equally potent triggers. He often feels a sense of unease when he can't predict or manage situations—such as when driving in heavy traffic—which amplifies his hypervigilance, making him jump at every unexpected noise. The sound of an exploding firecracker or even a loud car door slamming sends waves of fear through him. When these triggers are activated, Raj's memories come flooding back. He remembers the sensation of falling and the overwhelming grief he felt as he watched his home disintegrate around him. His body physically reenacts that moment, causing him to feel like he is reliving it once again. This visceral connection between the past and present makes the memory seem unreal yet excruciatingly real. Raj has come to believe that nothing in his life feels meaningful anymore. The trauma has shattered his sense of purpose as a painter, leaving him feeling no longer capable of doing the things that defined him. These negative appraisals have led him to ruminate constantly on why this event happened to him and how it changed everything he knew about himself and the world. In an attempt to cope with these overwhelming feelings, Raj keeps himself busy with work and avoids news reports that might remind him of the war. He believes that staying occupied helps mitigate the memories and triggers. However, this busyness often leads to exhaustion and only serves as a temporary distraction from the grief he feels when remembering the event. Raj’s hypervigilance is both a consequence and a driver of his negative appraisals and maladaptive strategies. His constant state of alertness makes him jump at every sound and smell, reinforcing his belief that the world is dangerous and unpredictable. This heightened sense of threat also exacerbates his grief and bodily reenactment when memories emerge. The interplay between these factors has created a self-reinforcing cycle for Raj. When he remembers the explosion, he feels overwhelmed by grief and a loss of meaning, which drives him to ruminate and avoid news. These maladaptive strategies offer fleeting relief but ultimately reinforce his negative beliefs about himself and the world around him. Raj's hyperactivity at work has taken its toll on both his health and relationships with his family. His wife often expresses concern over his constant need to be busy, which leaves little time for personal connections or rest. This tension in their relationship is just one of many consequences of Raj’s ongoing struggle with PTSD. What finally brought Raj to seek help was a particularly distressing episode at work where the sound of an industrial air compressor caused him to have a full-blown panic attack. His fear that he might be losing control and his hope for finding some peace and meaning in life again pushed him to reach out for support. Raj is most afraid of never being able to feel safe or regain his sense of purpose as a painter. He hopes therapy can help him navigate these fears and find ways to live with the memories without them constantly overwhelming him.
